nameStory: Mysis shrimp get their name from the Greek word 'mysis' meaning 'to close the eyes,' referring to how these tiny crustaceans seem to blink their stalked eyes as they swim. The species name 'stenolepis' means 'narrow scale,' describing the slender, scale-like plates that cover parts of their body.
description: Mysis stenolepis is a small, translucent freshwater shrimp that looks like a tiny glass ghost swimming through the water. These delicate crustaceans grow only about half an inch long and have a distinctly shrimp-like appearance with long antennae and multiple swimming legs. They're actually not true shrimp but belong to a group called mysid shrimp or opossum shrimp. Their nearly transparent bodies make them challenging to spot unless you look carefully in the right conditions.

idTips.label: Transparent body
idTips.description: Body is almost completely see-through like clear glass, with only faint whitish or grayish tints that shimmer as they move

idTips.label: Swimming motion
idTips.description: Moves with a distinctive jerky, darting motion through the water column, often in small groups that pulse together

idTips.label: Long antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of long, thread-like antennae that extend well beyond the head and wave constantly as they swim

idTips.label: Stalked eyes
idTips.description: Large, dark compound eyes mounted on short stalks that give them an almost alien appearance up close

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Tiny creatures measuring roughly 10-15mm (about half an inch) from head to tail tip

habitat: Found in the deeper, cooler waters of New England's larger lakes, particularly those connected to the Great Lakes system or with similar cold, clear conditions. They prefer the open water zone away from shore, typically staying in depths of 10 feet or more where temperatures remain cool year-round. Look for them in lakes like Champlain or other deep, oligotrophic waters with low nutrient levels.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters begin to warm, often rising closer to the surface during overcast days. This is when they're easiest to spot from shore.
seasonality.summer: Retreat to deeper, cooler waters during the day but may venture to shallower areas at dusk and dawn when surface temperatures drop.
seasonality.fall: Become more visible again as surface waters cool, with peak activity often occurring during the cooler months before ice formation.
seasonality.winter: Continue swimming beneath ice cover, though they're obviously impossible to observe from the surface during frozen periods.

funFact: Female Mysis stenolepis are actually 'marsupial shrimp' - they carry their developing babies in a special brood pouch under their body, just like a kangaroo carries its joey, making them one of the few crustaceans with this mammal-like parenting strategy!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with young fish fry or other small aquatic invertebrates, but the translucent body and distinctly shrimp-like shape with visible segmentation sets them apart. Remember: if it looks like a tiny glass shrimp darting through the water, it probably is one!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'shrimp,' mysids are not closely related to the shrimp you might eat at a restaurant. They're part of a completely different group of crustaceans and represent an ancient lineage that's remained relatively unchanged for millions of years.
compareHints: As the only Mysis species commonly found in New England waters, compare it to other small mysid shrimp in the family Mysidae, which tend to be marine species. Mysis stenolepis is distinguished by its freshwater habitat and slightly more robust body shape compared to its marine cousins. Other mysids you might encounter in coastal areas are typically smaller and more delicate-looking. **Note: Limited observation data (only 2 records) makes detailed comparison challenging.**
